what: The heuristic discovers customers and the depot from goal fact names, resolves their visited and loc facts once, and reconstructs a directed routing-cost matrix from grounded visit, return-to-depot, and visit-via-depot operator costs. At evaluation it identifies the current location and unvisited customers, computes an MST bound, a minimum-degree routing bound, and a discounted nearest-neighbor completion ending at the depot. The heuristic is the maximum of the structural bound and 90% of the greedy completion. If exact capacity, load, and all relevant demand PNEs survived translation, it also estimates the number of additional capacity-forced routes and adds a depot departure/return penalty. Missing optional resource PNEs simply disable that correction.
why: CVRP states are naturally represented as a current route endpoint plus a set of unvisited customers, so graph-based routing estimates provide much stronger guidance than counting goals. MST and degree bounds capture the global geometric structure, while the discounted nearest-neighbor completion distinguishes promising route prefixes and approximates the remaining tour cost without an expensive combinatorial solve. The representative instances use dense metric-like distance matrices and range from high-capacity few-route cases to low-capacity many-route cases, motivating both the routing relaxation and the optional capacity-induced depot-trip correction. Grounded operator costs are used because they remain reliable when travel-cost, capacity, or demand expressions are folded by the translator.
